chapter_theme: Under the heading சான்றோர் இயல்பு, twelve verses on the nature of the worthy: their worth shines through ruin, poverty and mud and is seen by the discerning; they keep their station in hunger, do not covet, give with knowing folly, speak no wounding word in company, judge their own hidden faults, shun slanderers, and pay for their height, since their faults are seen far and remembered long.

69.reading: Like a peerless gem that will not let the ash heaped over it cling and shows apart in its own brightness, the leading man, even when he is brought low, has a light of his own that matches a hundred thousand men.
69.nuance: The gem image says two things at once: the covering does not stick, and the shine is the gem's own, not lent by its setting. தாறாப் படினும் is obscure; it is read here as 'even if he falls into a reduced state', which the ash image supports, but the word cannot be fixed. The quotation marks take in the whole of lines 3-4, so the counsel and the proverb are one sentence.

pazhamozhi.proverb: தாறாப் படினும் தலைமகன் தன்னொளி நூறா யிரவர்க்கு நேர்
pazhamozhi.literal: even when he is brought down, a leader's own light is equal to a hundred thousand

story.act: no story; the proverb itself names the type, the foremost man whose worth outweighs a crowd

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the worth of the noble shows through any covering of low fortune

70.reading: Even when they have fallen into want, the exalted keep to the station they stood in, as a tiger, though famine-hunger torments it greatly, will not graze on grass.
70.nuance: The tiger does not refuse food; it refuses food beneath its kind. So the verse's point is not abstinence but keeping one's station: poverty may take the meal, it does not make the high stoop to what is low.

pazhamozhi.literal: however great its hunger, the tiger does not graze on grass

story.act: no story; the proverb is the tiger's nature taken as an instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the exalted hold to their standing in poverty

71.reading: As, when a mansion falls, its hall timber serves to raise another, so the great remain of great worth even when they have lost their standing, for what has no substance has no worth.
71.nuance: The image is of salvage: the house is gone but its timber is still good building stuff, so ruin strips the great of position, not of use. The proverb is read as ஈடு 'substance, strength' and பாடு 'worth, standing'; பாடு can also mean suffering or loss, which would give 'what has no substance has nothing to lose', and the verse's sense depends on the choice. கூடம் மரத்திற்குத் துப்பாகும் is compressed and the line's construction is not certain.

pazhamozhi.literal: to that which has no substance there is no worth

story.act: no story; the proverb states a rule of worth, read against the timber of a fallen mansion

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the great keep their worth when their status is gone, because it lay in their substance

72.reading: Whatever befalls those who rose high, the discerning recognise them as what they are, lord of the lovely hills, for to those who know, a gem stays a gem though it has rolled in the mire.
72.nuance: The weight falls on the knower, not the gem: உணர்பவர், உணர்வார்க்கு. Worth survives the mire only for an eye that can see it, so the verse is as much about discernment as about the noble. இணரோங்கி, read here as 'risen high, flourishing', is uncertain; it may refer to lineage.

pazhamozhi.literal: even when it has wallowed in mud, a gem turns out a gem

story.act: no story; the proverb is the gem in the mud

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the discerning see the noble's worth through any misfortune

73.reading: Even if they have learnt nothing, the well-born are far better than those who know other things, and there is no need to go and speak finely to them, for nobody sells sewing needles in the smiths' street.
73.nuance: The verse grants the well-born a knowledge that does not come by learning: to instruct them is to bring needles to the street where needles are made. It ranks lineage above schooling. குடிப்பிறந்தார் is a word of lineage rank, not of a named birth-group. Line 2 is read as மற்றொன்று அறிவாரின் 'than those who know something else'; as printed the line lacks a pulli and the comparison could also be 'they know another thing (of their own)'.

norm.note: a claim of the period that high lineage carries worth and knowledge without learning

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no one who sells sewing needles in the smiths' street

story.act: no story; the proverb is the trader who would bring wares to the place that makes them

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the well-born need no instruction, having what it would teach

74.reading: We have heard tell of those of old who gave a chariot to a jasmine creeper and a mantle to a peacock, lord of the shore of long waters where the pandanus flowers, and so, by that account, even foolishness done knowingly is an ornament to the worthy.
74.nuance: The verse does not deny that the gifts were foolish: a creeper cannot ride and a peacock is not cold. It calls the folly an ornament because it was knowing (அறி-மடம்), the act of a giver who saw the absurdity and gave anyway out of pity. The verse names neither giver.

pazhamozhi.literal: even knowing foolishness is an ornament to the worthy

story.act: givers of old who gave a chariot to a jasmine creeper and a mantle to a peacock
story.tradition: by tradition Pari (the chariot to the creeper) and Pekan (the mantle to the peacock); the verse names neither

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the givers' excessive gifts were knowing folly and so adorned them

75.reading: In the midst of an assembly of many, the worthy who keep to the right part will not say to anyone a word that lodges deep within, for, even if it were the tall one who guarded the herds of cattle, one who speaks will be spoken back to.
75.nuance: The restraint is argued from consequence, not from kindness: a wounding word in company draws a reply, and no rank, not even a god's, exempts the speaker. நிரைப்புறங் காத்த நெடியோன் points to Mal as the herdsman; the verse does not say which retort he received, and the proverb may simply set the highest case.

pazhamozhi.literal: if one speaks, one gets speech in return

story.act: even the tall one who guarded the herds of cattle would be answered if he spoke so
story.tradition: by tradition Krishna as the herdsman form of Mal; the episode of his being answered is not told

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a wounding word in an assembly brings a retort on any speaker, however great

76.reading: Looking only to the thought 'this is not fitting for me', being himself his own witness, the southern king thought on his fault and cut off his own hand, while it is those who think 'no one will see' who do unworthy deeds.
76.nuance: The proverb is a foil: it names the ignoble motive, secrecy, that the king's act refutes. He was unseen, there was no accuser, and he still judged and punished himself, so the standard is internal (எனக்குத் தகவன்று), not the fear of being seen. The counsel is general, the example a king's.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who did unworthy deeds did them thinking 'they will not see'

story.act: the Pandya king, judging his own fault with himself as witness, cut off his own hand
story.tradition: by tradition Porkai Pandiyan, who cut off the hand that had knocked at a house's door at night; the verse names only தென்னவன்

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the worthy judge their own faults though no one has seen them

77.reading: Before deceivers who have no fear at all of evil deeds and who speak lies and slander as if they were guarding one's interest, the worthy do not join in their words but turn away without fail, like a crow from a bow.
77.nuance: The slanderer's cover is concern (காப்பாரே போன்று): he backbites as if protecting the listener. The crow does not argue with the bow; it is gone at the sight of it. So the worthy do not refute such talk, they withdraw from it.

pazhamozhi.literal: like the crow with the bow

story.act: no story; the proverb is the crow's flight at the sight of a bow

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the worthy at once withdraw from slanderers who pose as protectors

78.reading: Even when hunger bends them double, the worthy do not set about desiring what belongs to others, lord of the great sea's shore where birds may nest in the palmyra fronds, for the sea and the forest never meet.
78.nuance: The proverb makes the separation a fact of nature, not an effort: the worthy and another's goods are as far apart as sea and forest. The shore with birds nesting in the palm fronds may hint that each kind has its own place.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no joining of the sea with the forest

story.act: no story; the proverb is the fixed separation of sea and forest

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the worthy do not covet others' goods even in hunger

79.reading: Faults in the exalted never pass out of talk, as the talk that clings to long-armed Mal who held women of rowed bangles never ends, lord of the hills where the wild cow suckles its calf, like the brand burnt on the back of a grey bull, which never fades.
79.nuance: The brand fades from no hide, but it shows most on a pale one: the grey bull, like the exalted, carries the mark visibly and for good. The Mal clause is hard: நிரைதொடி தாங்கிய is read as his holding (embracing) bangled women, the herding-god's dalliance, an old story that is never let drop; the episode cannot be fixed from the words.

pazhamozhi.literal: the brand set on the back of a grey bull, which does not fade

story.act: the talk about long-armed Mal and the bangled women he held is never dropped
story.tradition: by tradition Krishna among the herding women; the verse gives no more than the phrase

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a fault in the exalted is spoken of forever

80.reading: Though the small commit for many days faults grown hard and ripe, nothing at all ever shows in them, but a fault that befalls the exalted, even a single one, is a lamp set on a hill.
80.nuance: The verse is a contrast of visibility, not of guilt: the small man's many matured faults pass unseen, the great man's one is seen from everywhere. It does not say the small are better off morally, only that height exposes.

pazhamozhi.literal: a lamp placed on a hill

story.act: no story; the proverb is the lamp on the hilltop, seen from all around

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a single fault of the exalted is seen by all, while the many faults of the small go unseen

links.note: 69 says the noble's light is his own and the covering will not cling; 72 says it is the discerning who see the gem through the mud.
links.teaches: Read together, worth that survives misfortune needs two things: its own shine and an eye that can find it under the dirt, so the verse after 69 hands the burden from the noble to the beholder.

links.note: Naladiyar 300's tiger starves rather than eat a kill fallen on its left side; Pazhamozhi 70's tiger starves rather than graze grass. Both make the tiger's hunger the test of the excellent.
links.teaches: The two tigers refuse different things, one a proper meal improperly placed and one a meal beneath its kind, so honour is shown both in rejecting the base and in rejecting the ill-fitting.
links.list_adds: its proverb ties the refusal to poverty (ஒற்கம்) and to holding one's station, where the quatrain ties it to honour weighed against heaven.

links.note: Naladiyar 193 says a starving tiger will eat even a small frog and urges taking lowly work in need; Pazhamozhi 70 says the starving tiger will not graze grass and that the exalted keep their station in want. The conflict holds on reading 193 as counsel to stoop for a while.
links.teaches: The same starving tiger is made to argue both ways, so the pair shows where the line falls: the tiger may stoop to small meat but not to grass, stooping within one's kind but never out of it.
links.list_adds: it makes the tiger's refusal the proof that poverty must not move the high from their station, the opposite lesson from the same animal.

links.note: Kural 964 says those fallen from their position are like hair fallen from the head; Pazhamozhi 71 says the great keep their worth when their standing is gone, like the timber of a fallen mansion.
links.teaches: The pair splits on whether worth lies in place or in substance: the Kural's fallen hair is worthless off the head, the Pazhamozhi's timber is still building stuff off the ruin.
links.list_adds: its salvage image gives the fallen great a further use, where the couplet's hair has none once it leaves its place.

links.note: Naladiyar 347 says a gem-set golden sandal is still for the foot, so the base are known by their deeds though rich; Pazhamozhi 72 says a gem rolled in mud is still a gem to those who know.
links.teaches: Together they make one rule from both directions: wealth does not lift the base and mire does not lower the noble, so neither fortune changes what a person is.
links.list_adds: it gives the case the quatrain leaves out, the noble brought low, and adds that only the discerning see the worth through it.

links.note: Kural 409 says the unlearned, though born high, have not the worth of the learned born low; Pazhamozhi 73 says the well-born, though they learn nothing, are far better than those who know other things.
links.teaches: The two books rank the same pair, birth and learning, in opposite order, so the ethics group does not agree on whether lineage can stand in for study.
links.list_adds: its proverb makes the well-born the very source of what learning would bring them, so instruction is superfluous rather than merely outweighed.

links.note: Purananuru 200 presents Pari's daughters as the children of the man who gave his tall belled chariot to a jasmine creeper that never sang for him; Pazhamozhi 74 cites the same gift as hearsay of old givers.
links.teaches: The heroic poem uses the chariot to the creeper to claim a husband for the daughters, while the ethics verse turns the same act into a maxim that knowing folly adorns the worthy, so the patron's deed becomes a proof text.
links.list_adds: it sets Pari's chariot beside a second giver's mantle and names both as foolishness, a judgement the bardic poem never makes.

links.note: Purananuru 142 says Pekan is foolish (மடம்) only in giving, like rain on salt land, never foolish in battle; Pazhamozhi 74 says knowing foolishness (அறிமடம்) is an ornament to the worthy, citing the mantle given to a peacock.
links.teaches: The puram poem already calls Pekan's giving மடம் and limits it to the gift; the ethics verse adds அறி, knowing, and so makes the patron's folly a chosen virtue rather than a lapse.
links.list_adds: it pairs Pekan's mantle with Pari's chariot as one kind of act and gives the whole class a name, அறிமடம்.

links.note: Naladiyar 325 says it is a wonder if one who reviles another before an assembly survives when the reviled stays silent; Pazhamozhi 75 says the worthy say no wounding word in an assembly because any speaker is answered.
links.teaches: The quatrain gives the rare case, the reviled keeping silence, and the proverb the ordinary one, the retort, so between them reviling in company is shown to rebound whether it is answered or not.
links.list_adds: its proverb extends the rule to the highest speaker, Mal himself, so no rank exempts a reviler from reply.

links.note: Kural 293 says not to lie about what one's own heart knows, for the heart will burn its owner; Pazhamozhi 76 makes the king his own witness (தனக்குக் கரியாவான் தானாய்) who judges his hidden fault and cuts off his hand.
links.teaches: The Kural makes the heart the witness that punishes a lie; the Pazhamozhi shows a king acting on that witness and carrying out the sentence on his own body, so self-witness becomes self-justice.
links.list_adds: its proverb names the opposite motive, 'no one will see', and the story shows the inner witness overruling it in a king with no accuser.

links.note: Naladiyar 226 asks whether anyone cuts off his own hand because it poked his eye, to say one does not cast off a friend for a hurt; Pazhamozhi 76 praises a king who did cut off his own hand for its fault.
links.teaches: The same act is absurd as a response to a friend's offence and noble as a response to one's own moral fault, so the pair separates forgiving others from judging oneself.
links.list_adds: its story turns the quatrain's absurd hypothetical into a real and admired deed, by making the fault the king's own.

links.note: Naladiyar 189 says the pure in heart stay unshaken by cruel slander, like a lamp's inner flame; Pazhamozhi 77 says the worthy do not join slanderers who pose as protectors but turn away at once like a crow from a bow.
links.teaches: The quatrain gives the inner response to slander, steadiness, and the Pazhamozhi the outer one, flight, so the worthy are shown both unmoved by the slanderer and unwilling to stay in his company.
links.list_adds: it names the slanderer's disguise, speaking as if guarding one, and answers it with withdrawal rather than endurance.

links.note: Kural 174 says those of faultless sight who have conquered the senses will not covet on the plea 'we have nothing'; Pazhamozhi 78 says the worthy do not covet others' goods even when hunger bends them.
links.teaches: The Kural rules out need as an excuse by the coveter's self-mastery; the Pazhamozhi makes the distance between the worthy and another's goods a fact of nature, like sea and forest, so non-coveting appears as character, not effort.
links.list_adds: its proverb turns the couplet's conquest of the senses into a fixed separation that needs no struggle.

links.note: 79 says the fault of the exalted never stops being spoken of, like a brand on a grey bull; 80 says a single fault of the exalted is seen by all, like a lamp on a hill, while the small man's many go unseen.
links.teaches: Taken together, the fault of the great is exposed in both dimensions, lasting for all time in 79 and seen across all space in 80, which is why the heading asks more of them than of the small.

links.note: Kural 957 says a fault in the well-born stands out like the spot on the moon; Pazhamozhi 80 says one fault of the exalted is a lamp on a hill while the many faults of the small never show.
links.teaches: The Kural shows the fault against the bright moon; the Pazhamozhi adds the other side of the scale, that the small man's long-matured faults stay hidden, so visibility, not guilt, is what height changes.
links.list_adds: it sets the one fault of the great against the many of the small, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

source_issues: 77 line 1: the site's text lacks this line (தீப்பால் வினையினைத் தீரவும் அஞ்சாராய்க்); the reading follows the line as printed in our text.
69 line 3: தாறாப் is obscure, and the quotation marks open at தாறாப் படினும், taking in the counsel with the proverb.
73 line 2: மற்றொன றறிவாரின் lacks a pulli (probably மற்றொன்று அறிவாரின்).
76 line 2: தனக்குத் கரியாவான் has a doubled consonant that should probably be தனக்குக் கரியாவான்.
71 line 2: கூடம் மரத்திற்குத் துப்பாகும் is compressed and its construction uncertain.
